lesson.title: Mapping the Tree of Life
lesson.summary: Phylogenetics is the scientific study of evolutionary relationships among organisms, reconstructed as branching tree diagrams from shared characteristics, and today increasingly from DNA and protein sequence data.
lesson.body:
Phylogenetics is the branch of biology devoted to figuring out how different species, or larger groups of organisms, are related to one another through common ancestry, and to representing those relationships as a phylogeny, a branching, tree-like diagram that traces lines of descent back to shared ancestors. Every speciation event you have studied in this unit, whether allopatric or sympatric, whether it happened in isolation or as part of a burst of adaptive radiation, leaves behind a branch point in the tree of life. Phylogenetics is the discipline that tries to reconstruct where those branch points are and in what order they occurred, using evidence left behind in living and fossil organisms.

Historically, phylogenetic relationships were inferred mainly from comparative anatomy and the fossil record, looking at similarities and differences in body structure, developmental patterns, and the sequence in which fossils of different forms appear in rock layers. This approach still matters, especially for extinct organisms known only from fossils, but it runs into exactly the problem you saw in the chapter on convergent evolution: physical similarity does not always mean common ancestry, since unrelated lineages can independently evolve similar looking structures under similar selective pressures. This is precisely why the method you will study next, cladistics, insists on distinguishing shared derived characters, which do indicate common ancestry, from characters that are merely similar because of convergence or because they were retained unchanged from a very distant ancestor. Modern phylogenetics leans heavily on cladistic reasoning as its logical foundation.

Over the past several decades, phylogenetics has been transformed by the ability to read DNA and protein sequences directly. Because every heritable difference between species ultimately traces back to changes in genetic material, and because mutations accumulate in DNA over time at rates that can, within limits, be estimated, comparing DNA or protein sequences across species gives biologists an enormous, largely independent source of evidence for reconstructing relationships, one that does not rely on physical appearance at all. Molecular data has been especially valuable for resolving relationships between organisms that look very different from each other but are actually close relatives, or conversely, organisms that look superficially alike (as convergent evolution predicts they sometimes will) but turn out to be only distantly related once their DNA is compared. It has also allowed biologists to build phylogenies for microorganisms, such as bacteria and archaea, whose physical structures are often too simple to carry much useful comparative information on their own.

It is important to be honest about the limits of phylogenetic reconstruction. A phylogeny is always a hypothesis, an inferred best explanation given the evidence available, not a directly observed record of history in the way a family tree built from birth certificates would be. Different lines of evidence, anatomical, developmental, and molecular, sometimes point toward somewhat different trees, and phylogenies are regularly revised as new evidence, new fossils, or better analytical methods become available. This is a normal and healthy part of how the field works, not a sign that the underlying idea of common descent is in doubt, the basic pattern of nested, branching relationships among living things is about as well supported as any finding in biology, but the fine details of exactly which species are each other's closest relatives can and do get updated.

Bringing this back to speciation, a phylogeny is essentially a historical map of speciation events. Every place two branches diverge from a single point represents an ancestral population that split, through allopatric, sympatric, or some other mode of speciation, into two or more descendant lineages. Reading a phylogeny is therefore a way of reading evolutionary history itself, which is exactly why the next two chapters focus on cladistics and cladograms, the specific logical method and the specific diagram type that most modern phylogenetic trees are built from and interpreted through.
